articles.title: ‘Floor-collected, broken noodles used to make bhujia': What FSSAI found at Wai-Wai's Rajasthan unit
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has directed CG Foods India Pvt Ltd to stop production of its ‘Veg Bhujia Namkeen’.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has directed CG Foods India Pvt Ltd to stop production of its ‘Veg Bhujia Namkeen’ after an inspection at the company’s facility in Rajasthan found multiple food safety and hygiene violations.The food regulator said on Thursday that enforcement action had been initiated against the company over “unsafe processing, unlicensed bhujia manufacturing, and predated packaging”.During an inspection at the company’s unit in Roopangarh, Ajmer, officials found floor-collected and broken noodles being reprocessed into bhujia without heat treatment, FSSAI said.The inspection also uncovered the use of predated packaging and the unlicensed manufacture of ‘Wai-Wai MaMa’ and ‘Wai-Wai Mama Punte’ bhujia variants, allegedly in violation of Section 31(1) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.FSSAI said officials seized 32,107.2 kg of stock, including loose broken noodles, from the premises.The inspection further revealed deficiencies in hygiene and documentation, including inadequate pest-control records and other food safety lapses.Officials collected samples for laboratory testing and detained 1,925 boxes of expired finished products. Legal proceedings have also been initiated against the company.FSSAI directed CG Foods India to discontinue production of Veg Bhujia Namkeen products without the required approvals and corrective measures.The regulator said further action would be taken based on the laboratory test results and findings of the inspection.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: At 9, Yonas Hagos arrived in America from a Sudan refugee camp; years later, he became a major Arby’s franchise owner after serving in the US Army
articles.summary: US News: At nine years old, Yonas Hagos arrived in America after spending part of his childhood in a refugee camp in Sudan. He spoke little English and entered.
articles.body: At nine years old, Yonas Hagos arrived in America after spending part of his childhood in a refugee camp in Sudan. He spoke little English and entered a life that was dramatically different from the one his family had known. In Illinois, Hagos and his four siblings shared a small two-bedroom apartment with their parents, who worked whatever jobs they could find to support the family. As a teenager, he began working in fast food and taking on odd jobs to earn money. Years later, the attacks of September 11 changed the direction of his life. Hagos enlisted in the US Army in 2002 and eventually served in Iraq, where he was critically wounded by a rocket-propelled grenade. He survived, recovered and received the Purple Heart. After leaving the military, he pursued another childhood ambition, becoming a business owner, eventually building a multi-brand franchise operation that included Arby’s.Yonas Hagos arrived in America as a refugee childYonas Hagos' journey began long before he became a franchise owner. In 1992, he travelled with his parents and four siblings from a refugee camp in Sudan to Chicago, beginning a new life in America. Hagos was only nine years old and remembered being amazed by everything around him, from the size of American houses to the speed of the cars. His family settled in Wheaton, Illinois, in a two-bedroom Section 8 apartment, with the children sharing two twin beds. According to Inspire Brands, Hagos grew up poor but watched his parents work relentlessly to provide for their family. That example shaped his own attitude towards work. At 14, he obtained permission to take his first fast-food job and also earned money by shovelling driveways, cutting grass and taking whatever work was available.From fast-food worker to US Army Purple Heart recipientHagos continued working in restaurants while attending high school and college, but his path changed after the September 11 attacks. Wanting to give something back to the country that had given his family a new opportunity, he decided to join the US Army. He enlisted in 2002, serving overseas in Germany and Kuwait before being deployed to Iraq in 2004. During his final tour, Hagos was travelling through Baghdad in a Howitzer when his unit came under attack. An RPG struck the vehicle, leaving him severely wounded and without a detectable pulse. His comrades initially considered him killed in action before he regained consciousness nearly a minute later. He underwent numerous surgeries and began rehabilitation in Germany. Doctors initially told him he might have only 50% mobility, but after a difficult recovery he ultimately reached about 95%. Hagos received the Purple Heart Medal for his injuries.After the Army, Yonas Hagos pursued his dream of owning a businessSurviving his injuries gave Hagos a renewed determination to pursue the ambition he had carried since childhood, becoming a businessman. He first established a painting company to save enough money to enter the franchise industry. His first franchised business was a 24-hour health and fitness club, which he purchased in 2009. From there, his operation grew rapidly. At one point, Hagos owned 17 Dunkin’ restaurants, demonstrating that the discipline and persistence he developed during his military career could translate into entrepreneurship. He eventually expanded into other restaurant brands, including Smoothie King, Chicken Salad Chick and Arby’s. His experience was built gradually rather than overnight, with each business providing the foundation for the next. His approach was rooted in hard work, patience and a willingness to follow established systems while continuing to look for opportunities to grow.Yonas Hagos became an Arby’s franchise owner after growing up poorArby’s had a personal connection for Hagos because he had grown up eating at the chain in Wheaton. After hearing a business associate discuss the brand, he returned to an Arby’s restaurant, tried its brisket and began considering the company as another opportunity for expansion. He travelled to Atlanta to meet Arby’s leadership and said the brand's vision convinced him to become part of its growth. Hagos opened his first Arby’s restaurant in 2019. His story had by then travelled a remarkable distance, from a refugee camp in Sudan and a crowded apartment in Illinois to military service, a Purple Heart and ownership of multiple restaurant businesses. His journey is an example of perseverance and the possibilities created through franchising. His career demonstrates how a childhood shaped by poverty and displacement ultimately became the foundation for a life built around work, service and entrepreneurship.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: At 22, Theodore Roosevelt bought 155 acres in Oyster Bay; today, Sagamore Hill is a National Historic Site open to visitors
articles.summary: US News: Discover the fascinating history of Sagamore Hill, Theodore Roosevelt's family home and working farm, now a preserved National Historic Site open to visitors. Explore its rich legacy and the life of the 26th U.S. President.
articles.body: At 22, Theodore Roosevelt, who was the 26th President of the United States, purchased 155 acres in the Oyster Bay Cove area of Long Island. He bought the land for $30,000 and set in motion the creation of a home that would become Sagamore Hill. Eventually, the property was a reflection of several chapters of Roosevelt’s life: it was his family home, a working farm and, during his presidency, a summer base for conducting national affairs. Today, the estate is preserved as Sagamore Hill National Historic Site. The site does not still operate as a commercial farm, though. Instead, it is now preserved and interpreted for visitors.The journey from a 155-acre purchase to Sagamore HillReports suggest that Roosevelt had known Oyster Bay since he was a child, as he used to visit the Long Island area with his family during summer vacations in the 1870s. According to the National Park Service, he became attached to its natural setting and enjoyed activities such as hiking, rowing, swimming and riding. After finishing college, Roosevelt decided to purchase land in Oyster Bay, as he believed it to be the right place to settle and raise a family. He therefore bought farmland in Cove Neck and envisioned a substantial home on the property.In 1884, Roosevelt reportedly hired New York City architects Lamb and Rich to design a large Queen Anne-style residence, and the construction of the same began later that year. The plan, however, faced a major interruption when Roosevelt’s wife, Alice Hathaway Lee Roosevelt, died in February 1884, just two days after giving birth to their daughter, who was also named Alice. The house was eventually completed in 1885 by John A. Wood and Son at the cost of $16,975 after Roosevelt decided to proceed with the construction. He named the house Sagamore Hill.In 1886, Roosevelt became acquainted with Edith Kermit Carow, and the two got married later that year. Historical records show that Theodore and Edith took up full-time residence at Sagamore Hill in 1887, and would raise a total of six children, including his eldest daughter Alice, making the estate the centre of the Roosevelt family’s life for the following decades.Roosevelt had also dedicated 47 acres of the land to farmland, and the first buildings erected on the property were a stable and lodge that were constructed before the main house was built. The farmland included pasture and cultivated land that used to support the household. As per the federal organisation’s records, cows, chickens, turkeys and pigs were among the animals kept on the farm, while workers cultivated hay and straw alongside maintaining fruit and vegetable groves.A farm woven into the family lifeInstead of being an ornamental feature on the estate, the agricultural work was part of the household’s daily routine. Edith Roosevelt managed most of the property alongside the household responsibilities. NPS noted in their account that she would often send Roosevelt to help the farmhands bring in hay when she thought he was working too hard. Meanwhile, Roosevelt allegedly enjoyed the physical labour and reportedly even insisted the farm manager put his name on the time sheets so he could receive the daily wage after spending a day working alongside the employees.The farm’s size and production varied as Roosevelt bought and sold portions of the surrounding property to relatives between 1884 and 1906. The NPS currently describes the Sagamore Hill National Historic Site as protecting approximately 83 acres of the historic estate and its natural surroundings.The farm also accommodated Roosevelt’s growing political career. After becoming president in 1901, Roosevelt wanted to escape Washington’s summer heat and moved his office to Sagamore Hill during the warmer months. Therefore, from 1902 through 1908, the estate was considered his Summer White House for seven summers during his presidency, which eventually ended in 1909.Despite the presidential role, the property’s domestic character was left intact, as it continued to function as the Roosevelt family home while also hosting political meetings and esteemed guests. NPS noted that visitors staying with the Roosevelts could enjoy meals supplied in part by produce from the farm.Transformation from Roosevelt home to National Historic SiteRoosevelt remained at Sagamore Hill until his death on 6 January 1919, while Edith continued living there until her death in 1948. Theodore Roosevelt Jr., their eldest son, later acquired four acres from Edith in 1938 and built a house known as Old Orchard in an area that had once been the property’s apple orchard. This indicates that the property’s later history was not simply the preservation of one unchanged presidential residence, but the continuation of a family landscape that had evolved over generations.The federal organisation says that Sagamore Hill National Historic Site was officially authorised by Congress on July 25, 1962, with the land formally transferring to the government the following year. The preserved property now includes Roosevelt’s home and the surrounding landscape, allowing visitors to experience the setting in which the former president lived from the late 19th century until his death in the early 20th century.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Texas mom says school told her staff caught her 5-year-old son; she later learned a stranger found him crying two blocks away
articles.summary: US News: Kindergarten student leaves school without anyone noticing; a good Samaritan brings the child back after her ‘mom instincts’ kick in, but the school h.
articles.body: Kindergarten student leaves school without anyone noticing; a good Samaritan brings the child back after her ‘mom instincts’ kick in, but the school has a different storyA five-year-old kindergarten student in Texas left the school in the middle of the day without anyone noticing, before being found by a good Samaritan who safely returned the child to campus, WFAA reported.A good Samaritan helpsThe student, Elijah, left Rufino Mendoza Elementary School in Fort Worth, Texas, during school hours on Monday, August 31, NBC 5 reported. The child was later discovered by Isabel Barrera several blocks away, crying in the street. She was in the neighbourhood visiting her parents when she found him. She noticed the school name on the boy’s shirt and drove him back to campus, where staff told her they had no idea he was gone.“I see a little boy in the street; he’s running, crying, and I think my mom instincts just kicked in. He hugged me, and I hugged him back, and I was like, ‘Are you OK?’ And at that point, all I could think about was, he’s someone’s baby,” Barrera told the outlet.According to her, the school didn’t even know that the student had gone missing. “They’re like, OK, and everybody starts freaking out; they’re like, ‘Oh my God, we didn’t even know he got out,’” she added.The school has a different storyFort Worth ISD didn’t clarify how a student could leave the campus or how long the kindergartener was away from the school.“Fort Worth ISD is aware of an incident involving a kindergarten student who left campus during lunch on Monday. The student was safely located by a community member and promptly returned to school,” they said in a statement to WFAA. “The safety and well-being of our students remain our highest priority.”The district and campus administration are currently looking into the circumstances that led to the incident. Necessary steps to strengthen the existing safety protocols and procedures will be taken, according to the district.Mother demands actionThe child’s mother, Rebekah Alcaraz, said school officials gave her a completely different account when she arrived at pickup. “They said that he had walked out of the building but that two employees and the security guard had got to him before he was able to leave, and they brought him back inside,” she told NBC5.The mother later saw a post by Barrera’s husband in a neighbourhood Facebook group and realised that a stranger had found her son on the streets.Alcaraz and Elijah’s grandmother met with school and district staff on Tuesday, but they felt their concerns were not being taken seriously.“I feel like we’re being dismissed,” Alcaraz said.The mother added that the incident has left her worried about the safety of her son at the school. “They traumatized my little boy. They traumatized me as a parent, and I fear for his safety now at that school.”Though the school assured Barrera that the child’s family would be notified of the incident, the mother claims they didn’t tell her the whole story.“What they failed to tell me was that my son left the school campus. He was three to four blocks away from the school; he was crying and lost out there. And a parent that just so happened to have seen him was the one who brought him back. They didn’t notify me of any of this,” Alcaraz told the Fort Worth Star-Telegram.In the Facebook post, Barrera’s husband asked the school to do better on student safety protocols. “FWISD and Rufino Mendoza Elementary need to do better.”According to the outlet, the child’s mother has filed a police report and is also planning to seek legal action against the district. “It’s a parent’s worst nightmare, and it’s something you don’t think could ever happen to you until that happens to you. The fact that they’re not taking accountability still — that’s what’s really getting to me,” Alcaraz said.The incident has put a spotlight on whether the district’s heavily funded turnaround effort is reaching campus operations. For parents like Alcaraz, the money spent on teacher salaries and instructional overhauls means little if their child can walk out unnoticed.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1989, NBC anchor Tom Brokaw bought into a 4,000-acre Montana ranch; habitat work later helped upland bird populations return.
articles.summary: US News: Discover how NBC anchor Tom Brokaw transformed a 4,000-acre Montana ranch into a wildlife haven by restoring riverbanks and managing habitats effectively, leading to a resurgence of upland bird species.
articles.body: Tom Brokaw found an enduring connection to the natural world on a Montana ranch. In 1989, the then-NBC News anchor bought an interest in a roughly 4,000-acre property near the West Boulder River, seeking a place where he could escape the pace of broadcasting. What began as a private retreat became a long-term effort to manage land, restore habitat and observe how small changes affected wildlife.The Los Angeles Times confirmed in December 1989 that Brokaw had bought an interest in a 4,000-acre Montana ranch as a mountain retreat. The property was near the Absaroka-Beartooth Wilderness, an area known for mountain scenery and trout streams. Brokaw said at the time that he had been searching for property in Montana since visiting the state in 1981. The property eventually became known as the West Boulder Ranch. In a later interview with The Land Report, Brokaw explained that he had originally imagined buying only about 100 acres with a river. Instead, he and two partners acquired the much larger ranch. His wife Meredith eventually became equally attached to the property, and the couple later came to own it entirely.From retreat to restorationOwning a large ranch taught Brokaw that preserving a landscape was more complicated than simply leaving it alone. When he first became involved with the property, cattle had access to the river and grazed directly along its banks. Brokaw later recalled that he and his family began removing some fences and fencing off the riparian zone, allowing the vegetation beside the river to recover. They also tackled leafy spurge, an invasive plant that had become a problem on the ranch. Sheep and biological controls were among the approaches used to deal with it.Protecting the river corridor also affected habitat beyond the waterway. Riparian vegetation can provide food, shelter and nesting habitat for wildlife, while reducing livestock pressure can allow shrubs and grasses to recover. Research from Montana and elsewhere supports the broader ecological principle behind such work. According to a study published in Frontiers in Ecology and Evolution, increases in riparian vegetation, including woody plants, native grasses and forbs, were associated with greater bird diversity in mixed-grass prairie in north-central Montana. The researchers found that areas where this vegetation increased over time also showed increases in bird diversity, highlighting the importance of healthy riparian habitat for wildlife.When the birds returnedBrokaw's own observations became one of the most striking parts of the ranch's transformation. Working with a neighbour, he developed a project aimed at increasing the area's upland bird population. The approach was relatively modest. They planted about two acres of milo near wetlands to provide additional food and allowed grasses to grow taller in some of the ravines. Brokaw later said they noticed a substantial increase in birds, including Hungarian partridge, sharp-tailed grouse and other species. It is important, however, not to turn Brokaw's observation into a controlled scientific finding. There was no published experiment demonstrating that the riverbank work alone caused the increase. Rather, his account suggests that a combination of habitat protection, food availability, taller vegetation and changes in grazing management created conditions more favourable to birds. This matters because upland birds need a mosaic of habitat features rather than a single component. Montana guidance says sharp-tailed grouse prefer grasslands mixed with shrubs and riparian vegetation, while ruffed grouse use woodlands near streams.A different kind of celebrity landownerThe Land Report states that the Brokaw family owned West Boulder Ranch for nearly 30 years before selling the property on September 28, 2018. The 4,128-acre ranch, located at the base of Montana’s Absaroka Mountains and adjoining the Absaroka-Beartooth Wilderness, included about a mile of the West Boulder River and supported a wide range of wildlife, including elk, mule and white-tailed deer, antelope and Hungarian partridge. During the family’s ownership, the property became closely associated with Brokaw’s efforts to understand and manage the land as a working landscape. The sale, whose financial terms were not disclosed, brought an end to almost three decades of family ownership.Brokaw’s Montana experience became more than the purchase of a scenic retreat. Brokaw came to the ranch as an outsider drawn by its scenery, but soon took on the role of a land steward focused on the grass and the river. Brokaw’s story suggests that private ranches can become wildlife habitat when owners manage the river, vegetation and grazing as one ecosystem.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1989, Batman star Kim Basinger and her partners agreed to buy 1,700 acres of a Georgia town for $20 million; financial trouble later forced a sale for just $4.3 million
articles.summary: US News: Discover the story of Kim Basinger's bold investment in Braselton, Georgia, where her plans to transform the town into a film and tourism hub ultimately led to financial troubles. Explore the rise and fall of this Hollywood venture and how the town thrived after her departure.
articles.body: Hollywood stars are used to buying mansions, private islands and luxury cars. Kim Basinger went several steps further. At the height of her fame, the actress decided to invest in a small Georgia community, acquiring most of the privately owned property in Braselton for about $20 million. The ambitious plan was to transform the quiet town into a destination built around films, tourism, shops and entertainment. Within a few years, however, the dream had unravelled, and the property was eventually sold for just $4.3 million.According to the Los Angeles Times, the Braselton family agreed to sell about 1,700 acres to Basinger in March 1989, describing it as the bulk of the small northeast Georgia town. The piece of town was sold for $20 million in January 1990; it included a bank, an industrial park, 50 other buildings and two miles of Interstate highway frontage. Contemporary reporting by The Washington Post stated that the deal did not include the town's streets, cemetery or private residences. Braselton had about 500 residents at the time.A Hollywood dream in rural GeorgiaHowever, Basinger’s connection to the area was not entirely coincidental. She was born and raised in Athens, Georgia, and was familiar with North Georgia from her childhood. Braselton itself had a long-established history. The Braselton family had been closely associated with the community since William Harrison Braselton settled there in 1876, but by the late 1980s the town’s traditional commercial economy had weakened as shopping patterns changed and competition from larger centres increased.Plans discussed at the time included restoring older buildings, developing a tourist attraction, creating a film and recording centre and possibly staging a film festival. Planners also considered boutiques and other attractions that could turn Braselton into a destination rather than simply a small rural settlement. Basinger envisioned a large-scale entertainment and tourism development that would give the town a distinctive identity and attract visitors from outside the region.The idea of using film to draw visitors was not entirely fanciful. Research published in Tourism Management examined four UK locations featured in television productions and found evidence that screen exposure was followed by increases in visitor numbers. The study suggested that appearing on screen could help turn a location into a tourist attraction, providing some basis for Basinger's belief that a film-focused development could give Braselton a new identity.When the numbers stopped adding upThe problem was that publicity was easier to generate than a viable development plan. The proposed transformation never materialised on the scale originally imagined. The movie studio, recording facilities and tourist attractions remained largely plans. Instead of becoming a Hollywood outpost in Georgia, Braselton remained a small community best known for its celebrity investor. Los Angeles Times reports that at the same time, the investment became entangled with the financial difficulties that would eventually engulf Basinger. In 1993, she filed for bankruptcy following a costly legal dispute over the film Boxing Helena. A court had ordered her to pay millions of dollars after she withdrew from the project, although the judgment was later overturned on appeal. Her bankruptcy proceedings put pressure on her assets, including her interest in the Georgia venture. The Braselton investment ultimately ended in a steep loss. The partnership's property was sold in 1995 for about $4.3 million, a fraction of the roughly $20 million paid only a few years earlier. The figures represent a nominal loss of about $15.7 million, before considering financing costs and the division of the investment among the partners.The town that outlived the Hollywood gambleBraselton’s story, however, did not end with Basinger’s failed venture. The town went on to develop in its own right, attracting manufacturers, residential projects and businesses. The Mayfield Dairy Visitors Centre, Panoz Auto Development Company and a Havertys distribution centre became part of the area’s later economic landscape.In retrospect, Basinger’s risk looks all the more remarkable. She understood the possibilities a small Georgia town near Atlanta represented, but turning that idea into a major entertainment hub was much harder than expected. While her Hollywood background was enough to get her media attention and put Braselton on the map, there was no guarantee that her grand project would succeed. Therefore, Basinger’s Braselton experience stands out as one of Hollywood’s more unusual business ventures: an actress trying to develop a rural Georgia town into a destination for film, tourism and entertainment, and failing. Meanwhile, the town continued to grow long after Hollywood interest in it had faded.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Swatantra Bhardwaj to be arrested within 72 hours': CJP protester and daughter of assault victim
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: CJP protestor Nishu Azad on Friday said Delhi Police had assured her that action would be taken against Swatantra Bhardwaj within 72 hours,.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: CJP protestor Nishu Azad on Friday said Delhi Police had assured her that action would be taken against Swatantra Bhardwaj within 72 hours, as members of the Cockroach Janta Party gathered outside Parliament Street police station demanding strict action over the alleged assault on her father during a protest at Jantar Mantar.Speaking to reporters, Nishu said the incident had deeply affected her and alleged that she had also faced abuse and rape threats from Bhardwaj's supporters."Police officers have assured us that Swatantra will be arrested within 72 hours. They have promised to take action, and we hope there will be no further delay," she said."For days, his supporters have been abusing me and sending rape threats. I have filed an FIR against them as well. This incident affected me deeply. I stopped going to school for weeks and felt judged by everyone. I hope the police will now act and ensure that I do not have to suffer any further," Nishu added.Also read: ‘I could have been lynched’: Influencer Swatantra Bharadwaj clarifies ‘cracking skull’ claim during CJP protestThe protest outside Parliament Street police station saw CJP spokesperson Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka demand stringent action against Bhardwaj after a podcast clip went viral in which he purportedly spoke about the Jantar Mantar incident and his alleged political connections.The CJP delegation said it had approached the police seeking justice for Nishu and her father, Sanjay. Heavy police deployment was seen outside the police station.Ashutosh Ranka alleged that Sanjay was beaten during the Jantar Mantar protest and accused Delhi Police of failing to take adequate action."The criminal is openly admitting to the crime. We will demand that police register a murder case," Ranka said.Saurav Das also questioned why those accused in the case were allegedly moving freely and said the CJP would continue to press the police for action. Aazad Samaj Party (Kanshi Ram) MP Chandrashekhar Azad also joined the protest.The controversy centres on an alleged assault on Nishu's father during a protest at Jantar Mantar months ago. A viral podcast clip later triggered fresh outrage after Bhardwaj purportedly discussed the incident.Bhardwaj, however, has denied assaulting Sanjay and maintained that he acted in self-defence after being surrounded by a group of people."What people are calling an attack was an act of self-defence. If I had not acted in self-defence, I could have been lynched by the mob or killed," he said, claiming that he was surrounded by 10-15 people when the incident occurred.He also dismissed the viral podcast clip as fake and claimed that remarks about his political connections had been made sarcastically.Meanwhile, the DCP (New Delhi) said Sanjay's injuries were "simple in nature" and rejected claims that his skull had been fractured."The injuries were made by a kada and not by any weapon. The misinformation regarding crack in skull is not supported by facts or the MLC and is completely baseless," the DCP said.Police said a case had already been registered at Parliament Street police station and two individuals, including Bhardwaj, had been questioned. According to Delhi Police, Bhardwaj and another accused were served notices as per law and interrogated during the investigation.Police said due legal action had been taken and that a chargesheet would be filed before the competent court, while rejecting allegations of political influence or interference in the case.The issue had earlier escalated after Nishu posted a video claiming that her father required stitches following the alleged attack and expressing disappointment over the pace of the investigation. articles.title: Johnny Carson quietly left $156.5 million to his foundation after his 2005 death; by 2026, it was still funding Nebraska scholarships, arts and humanities
articles.summary: US News: Discover how Johnny Carson's $156 million legacy continues to benefit Nebraska universities and arts, enhancing scholarships and cultural programs two decades after his death in 2005.
articles.body: After his death on January 23, 2005, the foundation's directors knew a trust existed but had no clear sense of its size; they estimated its value at roughly one-tenth of what it eventually proved to be. According to Candid's Foundation Directory, the John W. Carson Foundation, which was created in 1981, was functioning over a period of more than two decades in the same manner as Carson himself, in that it was working discreetly by giving annual donations to children's charities and local organizations. It became known how much money was left by Carson in his last donation when the foundation filed Form 990-PF for fiscal year 2008.The filing was made with the IRS in May 2010 and first appeared that August, as reported by CNN Money. That filing disclosed a $156.5 million transfer from Carson's personal trust, split between $35.2 million in cash and $121.2 million in securities and royalty rights, a breakdown detailed in a foundation profile published by Influence Watch. With this disclosure, Carson's philanthropic group became the most well-funded Hollywood charity in the entire country, significantly ahead of other charities established by individuals in the entertainment business. The significance of this disclosure was not only because of the monetary amount involved. Carson had actually arranged the donation from a trust fund that he had established more than fifteen years prior to his death, meaning the trust had already been quietly building for more than fifteen years by the time it was disclosed.University of Nebraska-Lincoln gifts, 2004 to 2021Carson never lost sight of the state in which he spent his formative years, and he started contributing to his alma mater, the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, before his passing. According to the University of Nebraska‑Lincoln’s ‘Johnny Carson’s Gifts’ page and other university records, Carson and the Johnny Carson Foundation have contributed more than $16.5 million in total philanthropic support to the university. Major contributions to the institution were made in phases, starting with $5.3 million in 2004, aimed at supporting theatres and films; $5 million in 2005, coming from his estate, aimed at the endowment of theatres, films, and broadcasting; and finally, $1 million in 2010 and 2011 to start the Johnny Carson Opportunity Scholarship Fund. This fund was further enhanced, including an additional contribution of $250,000 in 2012 and $5 million in 2021.An announcement from the University of Nebraska-Lincoln Newsroom confirms that the 2021 addition was expected to extend annual scholarships to 50 to 60 students, worth roughly $300,000 in yearly aid, up from 15 to 25 students receiving about $100,000 before the increase. It led to the creation of the Johnny Carson School of Theatre and Film, and the Johnny Carson Center for Emerging Media Arts, all named after an individual who never had a press conference to unveil anything.The Nebraska cultural endowment's 1998 seed giftNebraska gifts of Carson went beyond his own alma mater. In 1998, he made a donation of $500,000 to establish the Nebraska Cultural Endowment, which is a public-private endowment in which philanthropic contributions are doubled by the state dollar-for-dollar. His contribution was a seed donation; the development of this endowment was due to further contributions and state matching. As of 2024, the Nebraska Cultural Endowment’s corpus stood at $30 million, split evenly between state‑held and privately managed portions, according to the endowment’s own ‘About’ page. Reporting in 2026 describes the fund as having a $30 million corpus that generates about $1 million annually for arts and humanities programming.In the same report, it is described that there is a 2026 budget threat where, due to a gap in excess of $471 million, the governor of Nebraska suggested that the $15 million state portion of the fund be moved to the general fund. The legislators decided to reduce the amount by $5 million instead of eliminating the fund.Foundation distributions two decades after Carson's deathBut there is another thing that makes the story of Carson’s giving remarkable. The money, amounting to $156.5 million from the trust fund, was not used for creating any eye-catching monuments. Instead, he established scholarship programs, an arts endowment, and academic centers all over the state where he had long been gone when he became famous.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Cardiff mum says 'no fat left to trim' as water bills set for 42% rise
articles.summary: Water companies were given the green light to increase bills for customers earlier this month.
articles.body:
A mum says there is "no more fat left to trim" off her household bills despite making changes at home to use less water.

Victoria Owen said she had implemented a "don't waste it" rule, encouraging her children to have short showers and re-use the water after washing dishes.

It comes after water companies across England and Wales were given the green light to increase bills for customers by an extra £3.4bn in the coming years, to meet increased pressures on infrastructure and the environment.

Welsh Water, Wales' main water and sewerage supplier, said it was working to support its most vulnerable customers and planned to invest £4.2bn by 2030 to improve services.

People in most parts of Wales faced a 27% increase in their water bills from April 2025, with the average annual bill going up from £503 to £639.

It marked the start of a five-year period of bill increases from Welsh Water, totalling 42% by 2029-30.

Pay more for your water bill or wait longer for a better service - new boss

Water bills set to rise for many after firms permitted extra funding

Victoria, from Cardiff, who is a single parent, said she spent "almost every single spare penny" on her household bills and there was "nothing left to waste", other than a Netflix subscription she had bought for her children.

She has a water meter, meaning suppliers charge a customer for the precise amount consumed rather than using an estimated flat rate.

"We turn the taps off when brushing our teeth, use the excess water on the plants after washing the dishes.

Victoria has introduced a shower timer to save water which has been "quite difficult" to enforce.

"My kids want to stand there under the shower for hours," she said.

"They've got a limited amount of time and then the hot tap goes on in the kitchen, which means they get showered with cold water."

In a survey conducted by the Office for National Statistics (ONS), 84% of respondents said they had taken at least one action to cut water usage over the past month.

Figures obtained by the Welsh Liberal Democrats revealed that Welsh Water lost 85,000 million litres of water due to leaks in 2024/2025.

Welsh Liberal Democrat David Chadwick has called on the water company to "urgently get its house in order" by fixing the leaky infrastructure.

Hafren Dyfrdwy, which serves the north east of Wales, lost 5,400 million litres of water in the same year.

A Welsh Water spokesperson said it was aiming to reduce leakage in its network by 24% by 2030.

It said it was investing £476m as part of a long-term project that would see the upgrade of the network over a period of years.

"Climate change is also impacting the situation as drying soil conditions increases bursts over the summer periods," it added.

Robert and Bernadette Guy, from Cardiff, said they were "absolutely shocked" to discover that their Welsh Water bill was set to rise by about £400 this year to £1,400 annually.

They decided to install a water meter which had proven more cost-effective - bringing their annual bill down to £600.

But Robert said this meant they were "having to think a bit more carefully" about their water usage.

"I've got a lot of pint glasses and every time I wash my hands in the sink, I put a pint glass below, and we line them up on on the windowsill before putting them on the garden.

"The other day I had seven pints of water which would have gone down the drain."

Robert said they were planning to buy a "dedicated bucket" to collect the water in the future.

"We've got a large garden and the thought of saying we can't afford to water it just felt awful," said Bernadette.

Bernadette said she was "absolutely astounded" to find out the cost of paying for their water, as it used to be just a "little add-on" to their monthly bills.

They said they felt it was also unfair to ask customers to take responsibility for years of under-investment into the ageing infrastructure .

"When I put the light switch on, I don't care how that electricity gets to my light bulb, I just want it to work," said Robert.

"I think that goes for a lot of people. We just want it to work when we want it and to work as cheaply as possible."

Prof Ian Walker, head of psychology at Swansea University, said people could be "constrained by automatic habits" when it comes to water usage.

He said: "You might think, 'I should take shorter showers', but once you get in there, you go into auto-pilot and take the same time regardless.

"One of the best things you could ask people to do is don't have showers and don't wash your clothes. But that's not going to happen either."

He suggested an easier approach was to lock-in water savings measures, such as getting a low-flow shower.

"You do that once as a deliberate choice, but then you never think about it again."

Welsh Water said its bills had "historically been held below inflation in real terms for much of the past decade".

"There is now a widely recognised need for increased investment to meet environmental requirements, respond to climate change and improve the resilience of our infrastructure.

"Customers pay an average of less than £2 a day for drinking water that is consistently ranked as equal highest quality in the world."

articles.title: How could US-Iran conflict end? Three experts give their views
articles.summary: After renewed strikes this week, does either side have an exit strategy?
articles.body:
The prospect of an imminent agreement to end the conflict between the US and Iran again seems unlikely, with the warring sides exchanging strikes and uncompromising rhetoric.

The attacks come days after the US said it was moving into a new phase - a sweeping economic blockade against Iran and countries which trade with it.

The US aim was to force Iran to negotiate and to stop its attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. The key commercial shipping route has been effectively closed since the US and Israel started the conflict in February.

A Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) the two sides signed in June and meant to result in a permanent ceasefire and a deal within 60 days has expired.

As the conflict enters its seventh month, we asked three experts for their thoughts on how it may play out.

US hopes military and economic pressure will weaken Iran's negotiating power

Jason Campbell , Senior Fellow at the Middle East Institute, Washington DC

The problem is we still do not know definitively what the US strategic objectives are in Iran. The White House is persistently re-evaluating what it is willing to live with from a political standpoint.

It was assumed the military component would be enough for a quick victory and that has not had the desired effect.

What we are seeing is different levers - both military and economic - that the US is trying to pull at.

Right now, the administration appears satisfied with some form of statis. I think they are satisfied with maintaining the blockade and with allowing some periodic targeting against Iran's capability to upset the shipping lane in the strait.

US officials are hopeful that the new sanctions will be enough to compel the Iranian regime to come to the negotiating table in a weaker position.

US forces have seemingly been able to facilitate a sufficient trickle through the Strait of Hormuz in recent days to avert an oil-price shock or a global economic collapse. But those were not the US objectives when starting the war.

My sense is that Iran is likely to demand a high price to get to a resolution, which is likely to remain politically untenable for the Trump administration.

Dr Aniseh Bassiri Tabrizi , Associate Fellow with Chatham House's Middle East and North Africa Programme, London

I do not think the latest strikes really alter Iranian calculations on the war. I think Tehran is preparing for an increased squeeze on its economy, and a continuation of the on and off attacks which we have seen over the past couple of months. Their intent will be to respond to these attacks in a proportionate manner in order not to spiral a larger conflict.

On the economic side, obviously this is likely to hurt the Iranian economy which has already been affected by the war and has had underlying structural issues anyway, as we know from the December and January demonstrations in Iran.

But I do not feel like there is the sense from the Iranian side that the economic squeeze is going to alter the Iranian calculation any time soon, including on any negotiations.

That does not mean Iran is not looking for an off ramp, but I think what we are seeing is that it is waiting for the US to go back to the MoU, or to at least offer some sort of concession. Tehran does not want to cave in to US pressure or alter its own approach in response to sanctions or additional attacks.

US knows what to do - go back to the ceasefire deal

Nicholas Hopton , Distinguished Fellow in international security at the Royal United Services Institute think tank in London and former UK ambassador to Iran

The latest spike in military action is not going to produce Iran's capitulation - it is just the latest twist. Economic pressure is also unlikely to work because China, Russia and many other countries which trade with Iran are not going to support unilateral US sanctions.

Iran can continue to disrupt the Strait of Hormuz - they have a thumb on the jugular of the global economy.

What is the White House's exit strategy?

Well, the US has already found it. If Trump was able to put a sustained effort into negotiating the deal outlined in June's MoU, that is the off-ramp.

Not only would a deal give the US a kind of victory because it would weaken the hardliners in the Islamic Republic, but also reassure everyone that Iran is not going to get a nuclear weapon.

There is a silver bullet in the MoU which is the lifting of all US sanctions on Iran.

What lifting those sanctions would do over time is weaken Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corp (IRGC). Economic engagement between the outside world and Iran in a new way would gradually force radical political and social change - so you end up with an Islamic regime, but of a very different nature.

Of course, that would not be straightforward to achieve, because of extensive IRGC penetration of the Iranian economy. But it should work, if given enough time and if the US and its partners exercised strategic patience which, sadly, is in short supply at this point.

For the time being, I think we're going to carry on with a messy, inconclusive situation that is bad for everyone.

articles.title: In 1965, scientists cut every tree in a New Hampshire watershed to determine how removing forest cover changes water supply; first-year streamflow rose about 40% and second-year nitrate topped 50 mg/L
articles.summary: US News: In 1965, scientists cut down all trees in a New Hampshire forest to study the effects on water supply, leading to a 40% rise in streamflow and alarming nitrate levels. This groundbreaking research changed perceptions of forests' roles in water dynamics.
articles.body: During the winter of 1965, a group of scientists conducted an experiment in the White Mountains of New Hampshire, which involved felling all trees within a forested watershed and leaving the fallen wood in place. The intention here was not to destroy but rather to measure the effects of such an experiment by studying how the roots and canopy of the forest interact with the water and nutrients passing through them. By completely clearing the vegetation off the watershed, scientists were able to study the process without any interference from a neighboring unmodified watershed.The results of this experiment changed the way hydrologists and ecologists thought of the role of the forests in general. As a result of felling all trees, the streamflow increased, the snowmelt occurred earlier and the concentration of nitrates in the stream rose to such levels that would not meet the drinking water requirements. In addition, the watershed used for this experiment is still under observation six decades later.Why scientists chose to clear an entire watershedThis location was Watershed 2 at the Hubbard Brook Experimental Forest, which the USDA Forest Service established in 1955 as an experimental research site to investigate the effect of forest cover on the quality and quantity of water, according to information on the USDA Forest Service Research & Development website. The researchers monitored the stream flow from several watersheds in the forest for years until they chose to clear vegetation completely in one of them for comparison with the other watersheds.All of the trees and shrubs in Watershed 2 had been cut down from November 18 to December 31, 1965, when there was more than 30 cm, which is about 12 inches, of snow on the ground, as recorded in the experiment’s official record provided by the Hubbard Brook Ecosystem Study. They cut stems and branches to one meter in height and all of the cut plants remained where they were, without moving the material offsite. There were no trails or roads, nor any vehicles in the study area, as they made an intentional effort not to disturb the ecosystem by cutting the vegetation and not to have logging equipment disturbing the soil as well. To prevent any re-colonization of this area by plants for the next three years, researchers used herbicides on this plot; first, bromacil was sprayed aerially in June 1966, then 2,4,5-T was applied to the ground in 1967 and 1968.Streamflow rose after the forest was cutThe impact of this process on the streamflow volume became evident very quickly. In the absence of trees that would normally pull water from the ground via their roots and transpire it into the air, a lot more rainfall ended up in the stream. The streamflow increased by about 40 percent during the first year after the cut, by 28 percent in the second one and by 26 percent in the third one, according to Hubbard Brook records. These numbers were reported in another peer-reviewed publication authored by Gene Likens et al., Effects of Forest Cutting and Herbicide Treatment on Nutrient Budgets in the Hubbard Brook Watershed-Ecosystem, and available in the free research archive maintained by the U.S. Department of Energy. It reported slightly more precise results for the first two years, 39 and 28 percent, respectively. Also, there was a shift in the date of snowmelt onset.Nitrate concentrations climbed sharply in Watershed 2Along with the flow change, there were massive changes in the chemical composition of the stream. Before cutting, nitrate concentrations in Watershed 2's stream did not exceed 1 milligram per liter. In the two years following, nitrate concentration reached the level of over 50 milligrams per liter, which Hubbard Brook's experimental records show. The peer-reviewed paper explains this phenomenon not in absolute numbers but in relative ones, noting that the level of nitrate concentration increased by 41 times in the first year and 56 times in the second year after cutting, which, according to the study's authors, caused the nitrate concentrations to surpass drinking water health limits consistently since cutting.The spike in nitrate concentrations is explained by changes in nitrogen cycling: with no trees to take up nitrogen, microbial mineralization and nitrification continued to convert organic nitrogen to nitrate, which then leached into the stream, a mechanism detailed in Hubbard Brook's nitrogen cycling research. Since all trees had been cut down, there was no vegetation left to take up nitrogen from the soil, so nitrogen was transformed by microorganisms into nitrate through nitrification and then ran off downstream without being absorbed. Besides nitrate, the increase was recorded in calcium, magnesium, potassium and sodium concentrations and in electrical conductivity; sulfate concentration was the only one to decrease.Six decades of monitoring followed the forest cuttingHowever, the purpose of the experiment was to allow the ecosystem to grow back on its own without herbicides after three growing seasons. As a result, scientists have gained decades of additional information on the dynamics of the recovery of the northern hardwood forest cut in Watershed 2. The Hubbard Brook Ecosystem Study, the results of which include this and many other experiments, became one of the most influential works on the environment in the twentieth century. One of them is the first evidence of the existence of acid rain in the precipitation of New England in the 1960s, which helped to pass the amendments to the Clean Air Act in 1990.Six decades after the last tree in Watershed 2 fell, the site is still part of the constantly monitored research forest. What used to be a drastic experiment in the complete deforestation of a plot turned into one of the best examples of how much work the roots and the crown of a forest ecosystem perform to retain water and nutrients, which becomes visible only after it ceases.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: In 2002, professor Ian Giddy and librarian Jenny Giddy bought a Costa Rican cattle farm to restore its cloud forest; 50,000 trees later, more than 300 bird species had been recorded
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Discover how Ian and Jenny Giddy transformed a degraded cattle farm in Costa Rica into a thriving nature reserve, home to over 305 bird species and all six wild cats of Costa Rica.
articles.body: In December 2001, Ian Giddy and his wife Genevieve (Jenny) climbed Cerro Chirripó, Costa Rica’s highest peak, purely for the challenge of it, according to the Cloudbridge project history and a 2023 Mongabay profile of the reserve. During their descent from the mountain’s height of 3,821 meters above sea level, they stopped and looked out at the valley, through which there appeared a rich cloud forest that suddenly ended at an exposed cattle pasture. Ian asked Jenny if they could come back and purchase that land.They actually followed their instincts and the following year they did just that. This spontaneous decision has evolved into one of the best-studied grassroots reforestation projects in Central America: a nature reserve that now houses over 300 bird species and all six of Costa Rica's wild cat species, on land that was once grazed by cattle.A 2002 land purchase born from a mountain hikeIan Giddy was a finance professor who spent much of his career at New York University’s Stern School of Business, according to his faculty page; Jenny Giddy previously worked as a research librarian for Environment Canada, as described in Cloudbridge project materials. None of them had any experience of tropical ecology at the time they acquired the first piece of land, which they did in 2002, acquiring a farm of about 60 hectares dedicated to cattle ranching close to Chirripó National Park, and which is a fact noted by the Cloudbridge Nature Reserve, where the couple founded their reserve. They gave the name Cloudbridge to their new piece of land, and over the next two decades, they bought six more farms. Mongabay, the independent non-profit news organization covering environmental stories, reported in 2023 that the reserve had grown to about 283 hectares (700 acres), while the Cloudbridge Nature Reserve's own website lists the total at closer to 200 hectares, plus an adjoining tract of virgin forest.Early failures and a change in strategyHowever, things did not work out well during the first attempts made by the couple to reforest the site. After three years of trying, they ended up losing almost 90% of the planted trees owing to the poor adaptation of the purchased seedlings from the commercial nursery to the high-altitude conditions at the site, as attested to by Tom Gode, president of the board of directors of the U.S.-based Cloud Forest Conservation Alliance (CFCA), the nonprofit that operates Cloudbridge Nature Reserve. Rather than giving up, the team tried a completely different approach to the task. Instead of buying the nursery stock, they began harvesting seeds from the adjacent old-growth forest and producing their own seedlings, which increased the survival rates of the planted trees to about 50%. Further improvements through the use of cardboard as mulch and mycorrhizal fungi in the soil saw the survival rates go up to about 90%.The team has also come up with an innovative way that is called island planting. Under this method, a small number of sturdy pioneer trees are planted in a completely barren field. Birds are attracted to the trees, and while perching on them, deposit seeds from other parts of the forest onto the ground below, eventually seeding a much larger area than the original planting covered. According to the Mongabay report mentioned above, the project has seen the planting of over 50,000 trees in more than two decades, which might not have been possible if bought from nurseries due to their poor survival rate.Two decades of returning wildlifeThe ecological payoff has been substantial. Jenny Giddy's colleagues recall that in the reserve's early years, sightings of birds were rare enough that staff could count the local species on one hand. As of the 2023 reporting period, staff at Cloudbridge had cataloged 305 bird species within the reserve, a figure Mongabay described as roughly a sixtyfold increase in under twenty years, and one that had already surpassed 270 species at an earlier point in the count. Among the returning species is the resplendent quetzal, a brightly colored cloud forest bird listed as near threatened by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.Mammal recovery has followed a similar trajectory. The reserve now hosts confirmed sightings of all six wild cat species found in Costa Rica: the oncilla, margay, jaguarundi, ocelot, puma, and jaguar, along with a resident female puma that has successfully raised young there, a sign researchers point to as evidence the forest can now support an apex predator. Camera traps have even recorded transient visits from the jaguar and from Baird's tapir, the largest wild land mammal in Central and South America, though researchers note the forest likely needs more time to mature before either species can be considered a true resident.A project that outlived its founderGiddy passed away in 2009 when he was 61, spending his last days balancing teaching finance in New York and paying visits to the reserve he had established along with Jenny. Jenny continued the project after his death, delivering speeches about their work in the United States and Canada, according to the memorial compiled for Ian Giddy by Cloudbridge staff. In 2019, she transferred ownership of the reserve to the Salish Coast Land and Marine Conservation Association, a U.S.-based nonprofit, while the Cloud Forest Conservation Alliance continued to manage day-to-day operations at the site. These days, Cloudbridge focuses on conservation, long-term research, and education rather than tree planting on a large scale, observing how the forest that did not exist two decades ago is growing year after year and developing into something similar to what Giddys saw above Chirripó.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Bristol woman sentenced after cousin killed in XL bully attack
articles.summary: Kelcie Reed admitted being in control of a dangerous dog which killed 19-year-old Morgan Dorsett.
articles.body:
A woman has been given a suspended sentence after an XL bully dog attacked and killed her cousin.

Kelcie Reed, 24, of Bristol, previously admitted being in charge of a dog dangerously out control , causing the death of Morgan Dorsett.

The 19-year-old, from Shrewsbury, died from neck injuries caused by the attack, which happened at Reed's flat in south Bristol in February 2025.

At Bristol Crown Court, Judge Anna Richardson sentenced Reed to 18 weeks in prison, suspended for 18 months. She will also be required to undergo mental health treatment.

Emergency services were called to a flat in Cobhorn Drive, Bishopsworth, to reports of the dog attack, but despite their best efforts, Morgan died from bites to her neck and face, a post-mortem examination ruled.

The dog, named Prince, was sedated at the scene and later "humanely destroyed", police said.

Reed, who appeared emotional throughout the proceedings, wept in the dock as the sentence was read out.

The judge told her: "Rather than putting everyone through the additional trauma of a trial, you accepted responsibility.

"You are someone who has over the last 18 months done what they needed to do to try and move forward. You need to continue to do that."

IDF dismantles over 30 weapon production machines in Nablus area during two-day counterterrorism operation.

Over 10 wanted individuals arrested and concealed weaponry confiscated by IDF guided by Shin Bet.

Prime Minister Netanyahu commends forces for successful operation in Samaria, vows to continue thwarting terrorism in various regions.

During the operation, the IDF, guided by the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency), also confiscated concealed weaponry, questioned suspects, and arrested over 10 wanted individuals.

The IDF dismantled over 30 weapon production machines in the Nablus area over the course of a two-day counterterrorism operation, the military announced on Friday.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu reacted to the operation in a statement released later on Friday.

"I commend our forces on a successful operation in Samaria in which they destroyed dozens of lathes for weapons manufacturing, seized dozens of weapons, and arrested individuals wanted for involvement in terrorism. Our activity to thwart terrorism continues with full force in Judea and Samaria, Gaza, Lebanon, and every place where our enemies attempt to threaten the State of Israel," the prime minister said.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Aristotle: "Man is by nature a political animal."
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Two people can think about human nature and reach very different conclusions about what a person fundamentally is. One imagines a self-contained indiv.
articles.body: Two people can think about human nature and reach very different conclusions about what a person fundamentally is. One imagines a self-contained individual who happens to live near other people out of convenience or necessity, but who could, in principle, be fully themselves alone. The other insists that living within a community isn't an optional add-on to human nature but part of its actual definition, that a person cut off entirely from society isn't simply a lonelier version of a complete human being, but something meaningfully incomplete. Aristotle, writing in his Politics, argued directly for the second view. The Greek term usually rendered "political animal," zoon politikon, doesn't mean political in the narrow, modern sense of elections and government. It means an animal whose nature is to live in a polis, an organised community, the way it's in a bee's nature to live in a hive. For Aristotle, humans outside of organised community life weren't simply unusual. He wrote that such a being would have to be either a beast or a god, since only creatures below or above the human condition could genuinely live self-sufficiently, alone.Quote of the day by Aristotle"Man is by nature a political animal."Written by a philosopher who never held citizenship in the city he analysedWhat gives this line an unexpected layer of complexity is Aristotle's own position within Athenian society while he wrote it. Though he spent decades teaching and working in Athens, first as a student at Plato's Academy for roughly twenty years and later founding his own school, the Lyceum, Aristotle was born in Stagira, in northern Greece, and as a foreign-born resident, a metic, he was never granted full Athenian citizenship, meaning he could never vote, hold office, or participate directly in the very political life his philosophy described as central to human flourishing. He built one of history's most influential theories of political community from a position permanently outside full membership in the specific community he lived and worked within.That outsider status became sharply relevant near the end of his life. After Alexander the Great, whom Aristotle had personally tutored, died in 323 BC, anti-Macedonian sentiment surged in Athens, and Aristotle, associated closely with Alexander, faced charges of impiety, the same accusation that had led to Socrates's execution decades earlier. Rather than stand trial, Aristotle left Athens for Chalcis, reportedly saying he did not want the city to "sin twice against philosophy." The philosopher who had argued communities were essential to human flourishing ultimately had to leave the community he'd spent most of his adult life in, to survive.A simple way to actually use this ideaThe useful move here is taking seriously the idea that isolation carries a real cost to human functioning, not simply an inconvenience but something closer to what Aristotle described: a departure from what humans are actually built for. Modern research on loneliness and social connection has repeatedly found measurable effects on both mental and physical health from prolonged isolation, a finding that lines up closely with Aristotle's much older claim, even though it arrives through entirely different methods.A fair test, when a period of isolation starts to feel normal or even preferable, is to ask honestly whether it's serving genuine needs or simply avoiding the harder, more demanding work of participating in a community. That question won't make community life easy. It usually clarifies whether withdrawal is a choice being made, or a habit that has quietly become mistaken for one.Other famous quotes by Aristotle"We are what we repeatedly do." "Knowing yourself is the beginning of all wisdom." "The whole is greater than the sum of its parts."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Ed Miliband says UK will 'resolutely uphold' Falkland Islands self-determination
articles.summary: The foreign secretary's comments come as Argentinian president Javier Milei says the "winds of change" favoured his country's claim on the British Overseas Territory.
articles.body:
The UK will "resolutely uphold" the self determination of the Falkland Islands, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said, after Argentinian president Javier Milei said his country needed to take them back.

Milei said the "winds of change" favoured Argentina's claim to the islands and pledged sanctions on firms planning to exploit close to the British overseas territory.

A British and Israeli partnership due to begin exploration work on the Sea Lion oilfield said it didn't expect recent developments to affect its work in the region.

Earlier Downing Street reaffirmed its position that the islands would remain a British Overseas Territory "for as long as the Islanders wish".

Argentine leader threatens to sanction oil firms and reiterates Falklands claim

Falklands is a pressure point for the UK – and the US knows it

More than 40 years after the war over the territory, sovereignty of the archipelago in the south-west Atlantic Ocean remains hotly disputed between Britain and Argentina.

However in a 2013 referendum, residents of the islands voted overwhelmingly to remain a British overseas territory - with 99.8% voting in favour and just three voting against.

Announcing his plan for sanctions in a national address on Thursday, Milei reiterated that the Falkland Islands were "historically and legally" Argentinian.

Milei described the Sea Lion oilfield as a "clear and present danger", and said if Argentina does not act swiftly, "they will have the material capacity to access the oil that lies underneath our sea – something that has never happened before."

It is not yet clear how or to what extent the sanctions will be imposed or tightened. In Argentina, a current law already allows for restrictions of activities of oil companies participating in projects considered unauthorised on the islands.

Two oil companies – Britain's Rockhopper Exploration and Israel's Navitas Petroleum – are due to begin extracting oil in the Sea Lion oilfield off the Falklands coast within two years, something Milei said Argentina could not allow.

A joint statement from the two firms on Friday said it had the valid licences granted by the government of the Falkland Islands, "and with the full support of the UK government."

The project is due to deliver its first oil in 2028, Rockhopper and Navitas said the partnerships' timetable would not be affected.

The Sea Lion oilfield, around 130 miles from the islands, contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil - described by Rockhopper as a field containing "highly marketable crude".

In comparison, the Rosebank oil field 80 miles west of the Shetland islands in the North Sea, contains an estimated 300 million barrels .

On Thursday, President Trump hinted the US would not help the UK in any future Falklands conflict because Britain "had not been there to help me" during his war with Iran.

Trump's latest remarks on the islands come after he previously said the US position on the Falklands is one of many under review .

Writing on X on Friday, Miliband said the Islands would remain British as that is the "overwhelming position of the islanders."

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting also said Britain's commitment to the Falkland Islands was "absolute and unshakeable".

"Milei's statement overnight tells us more about domestic politics in Argentina than it does about the Falkland Islands," he wrote in his own post on X.

Downing Street's statement said it was "not the first time" the Argentine government had made economic threats against the Falkland Islands.

"We are clear that the Falkland Islanders' right of self-determination extends to the right to exploit their own natural resources," it said.

articles.title: Uganda's King Oyo death: Body of world's youngest traditional monarch returns amid succession row
articles.summary: King Oyo died in the US last week aged 34 after receiving treatment for an aggressive form of cancer.
articles.body:
The body of a popular traditional ruler who was world's youngest reigning monarch has been flown home to Uganda where President Yoweri Musveni was amongst the mourners gathered at Entebbe airport to pay their respects.

The Tooro king will be buried next Saturday - the day he had hoped to celebrate the anniversary of his coronation. He had ascended the throne aged just three and was crowned when he turned 18.

The return of his body marks the start of the Tooro kingdom's official nine-day mourning period amid a growing public dispute over who should succeed him.

Uganda is governed by an elected president and parliament, but it has several traditional kingdoms that continue to have significant cultural influence despite not having political power.

Oyo, who Guinness World Records listed as the world's youngest reigning monarch , ruled over more than two million people. He was the 13th monarch of a kingdom that was founded in the early 19th Century.

After a brief ceremony at the airport, his body was flown by military helicopter to Kyegegwa in western Uganda, where the Tooro Kingdom is located, before being taken by road to the royal palace in Fort Portal.

It will lie in state at Karuziika Palace for the mourning period and members of the public will be allowed to pay their respects and prayers will be held there each evening.

On Thursday, Uganda's parliament held a special tribute to King Oyo, with MPs remembering him as a modernising monarch who championed education, health and opportunities for young people.

Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja described him as a "symbol of unity" and praised his work raising awareness about HIV and Aids among young people.

Opposition MPs also paid tribute, with acting opposition leader Patrick Nsamba Oshabe saying: "Heritage and development were never rivals in his hands."

President Museveni has ordered an official burial for the monarch and national flags will fly at half-mast for three days around the funeral.

On Wednesday, the Tooro kingdom's Prime Minister, Calvin Armstrong Rwomiire Akiiki, said the king had asked officials not to disclose the seriousness of his illness because he believed he would recover and return to his people.

He said the monarch had hoped to return home for this year's Empango - the annual celebration of his coronation - on 12 September.

"He was confident in his recovery," Akiiki said.

His death has triggered uncertainty over the future of the monarchy as Oyo was not officially married.

But Akiiki has said the king had a young son, whose identity would be revealed later in accordance with Tooro customs.

President Museveni also said the king's mother, Queen Best Kemigisa, had told him that her son had left an heir.

But Charles Kamurasi, who is head of the Babiito royal clan from which Tooro's kings are chosen, said he knew nothing about the reported child, prompting an unusual public disagreement among senior figures in the kingdom.

Others within the royal clan have questioned why they were apparently unaware of the child.

"The prime minister is not supposed to talk about the king's heir. It is a cultural process," one royal clan member was quoted as saying by Uganda's state-owned New Vision newspaper.

"How can we, blood relatives, not know of the child, and the prime minister says he knows? That is totally out of order," the clan member added.

Akiiki has since appealed for the dispute to be dealt with privately, saying he wanted to meet other elders to resolve their differences.

"Words spoken in moments of grief can deepen divisions that may take years to repair," he warned.

The Ugandan government has also intervened, urging people not to spread speculation about the succession on social media.

Culture Minister Henry Tumukunde said Ugandans should rely on official information from the government and the Tooro Kingdom, adding that any dispute would be dealt with under law governing traditional and cultural leaders.

"The whole world is watching how Uganda mourns its king," he said, urging people to show "restraint and respect".

The Tooro Kingdom follows a hereditary system in selecting its monarch.

King Oyo ascended the throne in 1995 and became an international curiosity because of his young age.

Before his burial, a church funeral service will be held at a local church.

His body will then be carried in a traditional procession to the Karambi Royal Tombs, with burial is expected to be completed by 14:00 local time.

According to Tooro tradition, kings are not buried in the evening.

articles.title: Human Remains Found During Search for Missing Dad, 40, Who Vanished 8 Months Ago
articles.summary: Joshua Clifton-Demell was last seen in South Australia on Jan. 23
articles.body:
Human remains were found near where Joshua Clifton-Demell's motorbike was discovered abandoned in January

Police are conducting forensic testing to confirm the identity and have informed Clifton-Demell's family of the discovery

The 40-year-old father was last seen on a motorbike in South Australia, on Jan. 23

A dad missing for over eight months is feared dead after human remains were found during the search for him in Australia.

On the morning of Friday, Sept. 4, police discovered human remains near Yorkeys Crossing in a remote region of South Australia amid a renewed effort to find Joshua Clifton-Demell, local outlets the Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC), 9 News and 7 News reported. The location is close to where Clifton-Demell's motorbike was found abandoned on a dirt track on Jan. 24.

"It is too early to confirm the identity of the human remains. They will be subject to forensic testing and I hope to have the results in the coming days," said Superintendent Josh Heinze, per ABC. "As soon as the identity of the human remains is confirmed, police will provide a further update."

Clifton-Demell, 40, was last seen leaving an address in the outback town of Port Augusta West on a motorbike at around 6 p.m. local time on Friday, Jan. 23, according to the National Missing Persons Coordination Centre .

At the time of his disappearance, South Australia Police described him in a Facebook post as 5 feet 7 inches tall "with a stocky build, mullet-style haircut and brown eyes. He has a large cross tattooed on the right side of his neck."

"Police hold grave concerns for his safety," they added.

According to ABC, police have been in contact with Clifton-Demell's family to inform them that human remains were found in the area of his disappearance. The matter is not currently being treated as suspicious.

The findings come as Major Crime and Missing Persons Investigation Section officers joined the Mounted Operations Unit, SES volunteers, local detectives and aerial support in extending the search for Clifton-Demell earlier this week, 7 News and 9 News reported.

His brother, Tim Clifton, was among the last people to see him before he vanished.

"Went out for a motorbike ride with one of our cousins, and he never returned," Clifton told 9 News previously. "They found the motorbike and never found him. It's been hell, really thinking about what happened to my brother."

Clifton-Demell's wife, Shelby Clifton-Demell, told the outlet that she knew something was wrong when they still hadn't received contact from him by their 6-year-old daughter Kiani's birthday on Feb. 2.

"It's been pure hell, emotional. I've never felt as empty as I feel now," said Shelby, per 9 News.

"It just breaks my heart when she says, 'What if daddy has forgotten about me, Mom?' I tell her, 'he'd never forget about you,'" she continued, referring to her daughter.

Want to keep up with the latest crime coverage? Sign up for PEOPLE's free True Crime newsletter for breaking crime news, ongoing trial coverage and details of intriguing unsolved cases.

The initial search for Clifton-Demell earlier this year was called off after two weeks.

"I'm glad the search has started up again, I really am and I'm glad they're taking certain things reported seriously," said Shelby. "He was my best friend. I need closure for myself and my daughter."

South Australia Police did not immediately respond to PEOPLE's request for comment.

articles.title: In 1905, a Maryland stone mansion was built on nearly 9 wooded acres; after John Harbaugh bought it for $3 million in 2013, the former Ravens coach has now sold it for $6 million
articles.summary: US News: Former Baltimore Ravens head coach John Harbaugh has sold his historic Maryland home for $6 million, ending another connection to the city after 18 se.
articles.body: Former Baltimore Ravens head coach John Harbaugh has sold his historic Maryland home for $6 million, ending another connection to the city after 18 seasons with the NFL team.The stone mansion is located in Owings Mills, a suburb about 20 minutes from Baltimore. According to Mansion Global, Harbaugh had owned the property since November 2013, when he bought it for $3 million through a trust, according to PropertyShark records.The sale means Harbaugh received exactly twice the amount he paid for the home. He had put the property on the market in May for $6.9 million before it eventually sold for $6 million.Harbaugh bought the home in the same year that he led the Ravens to their second Super Bowl victory. He remained with the team for 18 seasons before being fired at the end of last season. The Ravens finished the season 8-9 and missed the playoffs.Moving on from BaltimoreThe 63-year-old coach has since taken up a new role with the New York Giants. The team hired him as its head coach in January, and he signed a five-year contract reportedly worth $20 million per season.With the new job now under way, Harbaugh and his family have also moved to New Jersey, where the Giants are based. The Baltimore Sun reported last month that the family had moved into a home in the Garden State.The Maryland mansion therefore became one of the remaining links between Harbaugh and the city where he spent nearly two decades coaching the Ravens. Details about the buyer of the property are unknown. The buyer was represented by JoAnn Rostek of Cummings & Co. Realtors.A 1905 stone mansionThe property dates back to 1905 and sits on nearly nine wooded acres. According to its listing, the historic stone house was renovated by Maryland-based Delbert Adams Construction Group.The traditional-style home covers more than 9,100 square feet across four levels. It has five bedrooms, including a primary suite on the second floor with its own sitting room.The property also has a detached carriage house, which provides enough space to add a sixth bedroom. The carriage house has its own kitchen, family room and full bathroom, giving it a separate living space within the property.A loft above the four-car garage adds another flexible area. According to the listing, the space could be used as a gym, office or guest suite.Outdoor include pool, patiosThe home also offers several outdoor spaces. The rear of the house opens onto a bluestone patio with a sitting area and fireplace.Another patio leads to the pool area. The outdoor space includes a hot tub and a pool house, adding to the property's recreational facilities.The combination of the historic stone exterior, large wooded grounds and extensive interior space made the property a sizeable home for Harbaugh during his years in Maryland.Harbaugh's ownership also covered a major period in his Ravens career. He purchased the mansion after leading Baltimore to its Super Bowl victory in 2013 and continued living in the area through the rest of his tenure with the team. His departure from the Ravens came after the 2025 season, when the team finished with eight wins and nine losses.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
